result: Transgenic C. reinhardtii strains expressing FP-tagged IFT proteins display normal flagellar morphology and IFT dynamics, with distinct spatial distributions of different IFT proteins in the basal body pool.
evaluation: Claims C28-C35 collectively demonstrate that the FP-tagged strains are functional (normal flagellar length, wild-type IFT velocities and frequencies) and that different IFT proteins occupy distinct spatial domains in the bb-pool. The data are supported by Figure 1 showing flagellar length, IFT velocities, frequencies, and imaging of protein distributions.

result: FRAP analysis reveals that IFT proteins in the basal body pool exchange at different rates, with KAP-GFP recovering in less than 4 s while IFT-B proteins require ~9 s for maximum recovery.
evaluation: Claims C36-C41 are supported by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 2. The differential recovery times (C39, C40) and the conclusion that IFT proteins exchange at different rates (C41) are directly supported by quantitative data with appropriate sample sizes (n=14-28) and statistical analysis.

result: FLIP experiments demonstrate that IFT-B proteins (IFT20/46/54) reenter the basal body pool after retrograde transport, while IFT-A proteins and motor subunits do not, indicating differential recycling of IFT subcomplexes.
evaluation: Claims C42-C49 are supported by FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3. The differential fluorescence loss between IFT-B proteins (significant loss) and IFT-A/motor proteins (minimal loss) is quantified with appropriate controls and sample sizes. The plateau at ~52% for NG-IFT54 (C46) provides quantitative support for partial recycling.

result: During prolonged FLIP, anterograde trains continue to enter the experimental flagellum with reduced signal intensity, indicating that trains contain both bleached proteins from retrograde trains and unbleached proteins recruited from the cell body.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by quantitative analysis of train signal intensity during FLIP experiments. The 40% intensity decrease for NG-IFT54 trains (C53) compared to 10% for IFT43-YFP (C52) provides quantitative evidence for the mixed composition of anterograde trains, supporting the semi-open system model.

result: C. reinhardtii possesses a largely open IFT system where IFT-A and motor proteins are recruited from the cell body, cycle once through the flagellum, and return to the cell body, while IFT-B proteins are partially recycled in a semi-open system.
evaluation: Claims C55, C2, and C3 represent the major conclusion of the manuscript, supported by the combined FRAP and FLIP data (Figures 2-3). The distinction between open (IFT-A, motors) and semi-open (IFT-B) systems is well-supported by differential fluorescence loss patterns and train intensity measurements.

result: Prolonged FLIP bleaching of one ciliary tip progressively depletes the entire cellular IFT-FP pool in both cilia, with unbleached proteins evenly distributed between flagella, indicating mixing in the cell body pool and stochastic recruitment to basal bodies.
evaluation: Claims C56-C59 are supported by prolonged FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The even distribution of unbleached NG-IFT54 between flagella (C58) and the 6-9 minute depletion time (C57) support the conclusion of mixing in the cb-pool and stochastic recruitment (C59).

result: Total flagella bleaching experiments reveal that ~50% of NG-IFT54 in the basal body pool is derived from retrograde trains, with a residence time of ~6 s in the pool before release or reuse.
evaluation: Claims C60-C64 are supported by total flagella FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3. The 52% decline in bb-pool signal (C60) directly supports the 50% recycling estimate (C61). The residence time calculation (C64) is based on the difference between retrograde train return time (10.9 s, C62) and pool recovery time (16.6 s, C63), which is a reasonable inference.

result: KAP-GFP and IFT43-YFP (IFT-A) are released into the cell body pool upon return from the cilium, as their basal body pool signal remains unaltered after total flagella bleaching.
evaluation: Claim C65 is supported by total flagella FLIP experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E-H. The lack of change in bb-pool signal for KAP-GFP and IFT43-YFP contrasts with the 52% decline observed for NG-IFT54, providing strong evidence for differential recycling behavior.

result: FRAP analysis in IMCD3 cells and T. thermophila reveals open and semi-open IFT systems similar to C. reinhardtii, with basal body pool recovery and resumption of fluorescent IFT traffic within 16-29 seconds.
evaluation: Claims C66-C71 are supported by FRAP experiments in IMCD cells (Figure 4A-C) and T. thermophila (Figure 4D-F). The recovery times (16.8 s for IMCD, 29 s for Tetrahymena) and appearance of unbleached trains (18.1 s and 17.1 s respectively) demonstrate continuous recruitment from the cell body, supporting open/semi-open systems across species.

result: The departure or arrival of a single IFT train causes a 12-16% change in basal body pool signal strength, indicating that the pool contains the equivalent of approximately 6-8 IFT trains.
evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5A-C. The 16.1% decrease for KAP-GFP and 12.7% for NG-IFT54 upon train departure (C72) directly supports the inference that the pool contains 6-8 train equivalents (C74), assuming each train represents 12-16% of the pool signal.

result: IFT trains exit the basal body pool from distinct sites, resulting in local depletion, and consecutive trains are often released from different sites.
evaluation: Claims C75-C76 are supported by imaging observations shown in Figure 5D-I and Video 6. The merged kymograms from different scanning positions (Figure 5E-I) demonstrate that consecutive trains exit from distinct sites, though no particular pattern was observed.

result: Gap analysis after bleaching the basal body pool reveals that different IFT proteins have distinct transition times through the pool (2.5-7 s), with significant differences between IFT-A/B1 and motor proteins, indicating sequential recruitment of IFT subcomplexes.
evaluation: Claims C77-C83 are supported by gap analysis experiments shown in Figure 6. The range of gap durations (C80) and statistical analysis showing significant differences between IFT-A/B1 and motors (C82) but not within subcomplexes (C81) support the conclusion of sequential recruitment (C83, C5). Sample sizes are adequate (n=17-60).

result: Two-color gap and FRAP analysis demonstrates that IFT140 (IFT-A) is recruited early during train assembly while KAP (kinesin-2) is added later, supporting a model of sequential assembly with trains in different stages queuing at the basal body.
evaluation: Claims C84-C90 are supported by two-color experiments shown in Figure 7. The observation that KAP-GFP trains appear before KAP-GFP+IFT140-mCherry trains in 42/49 experiments (C84) and the differential FRAP recovery (C87) provide strong evidence for sequential recruitment (C88). This supports the main conclusion (C7, C90) of trains in multiple assembly stages queuing for release.

result: Gap analysis of sfGFP-tubulin and D1bLIC reveals very short gaps (1.9-2.5 s) after basal body bleaching, indicating that tubulin and IFT dynein cargoes are loaded briefly before train departure into the cilium.
evaluation: Claims C91-C95 are supported by gap analysis of sfGFP-tubulin shown in Figure 8C-D. The short gap durations (1.9-2.5 s) for tubulin and D1bLIC are significantly shorter than those for IFT particle proteins (2.5-7 s), supporting the conclusion that cargo loading occurs late in train assembly (C95, C6, C124). The lack of significant difference between experimental and control flagella (p=0.74, C92) strengthens the conclusion.

result: Based on the ~9 s gap duration for IFT-A/B2 proteins and the ~1/s train exit frequency, approximately 9 trains in different stages of assembly are present in the basal body pool at any given time.
evaluation: Claims C113-C115 represent a quantitative inference based on gap analysis (Figure 6C) and IFT frequency measurements (Figure 1D). The calculation that ~9 trains are in the pool (C115) is a reasonable inference from the 9 s gap duration (C113) and 1/s frequency (C114), though this assumes continuous assembly and no gaps between trains.

result: A speculative model proposes that each of the nine basal body triplets assists in assembling one IFT train, with nascent trains moving upward along triplet blades, combining with subcomplexes, and associating with kinesin-2 at the transitional fibers before entry into the cilium.
evaluation: Claims C116-C119 represent a speculative model (explicitly stated as such in C116) that attempts to explain the observed ~9 trains in the pool. While the model is consistent with the data, it lacks direct experimental support. The model integrates structural knowledge of basal bodies with the functional data, but alternative explanations are possible.

result: Prior work in T. brucei and C. elegans proposed closed IFT systems where proteins cycle between the flagellum and basal body pool with limited exchange with the cell body, contrasting with the open system observed in C. reinhardtii.
evaluation: Claims C100-C103 accurately describe prior work from Buisson et al., 2013 (T. brucei) and Mijalkovic et al., 2017; Prevo et al., 2015 (C. elegans). These claims are properly cited and provide important context for the current findings, highlighting species-specific differences in IFT dynamics.

result: The bulk of motor subunits in C. reinhardtii anterograde trains is recruited from the cell body pool, unlike the closed system in C. elegans, which may be related to structural differences in mature C. elegans cilia that lack transitional fibers.
evaluation: Claims C104-C106 integrate the current findings (C104, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3G,H) with prior structural knowledge about C. elegans cilia (C105, cited to Nechipurenko et al., 2017). The speculation about transitional fibers being critical for recruitment (C106) is reasonable but lacks direct experimental support.

result: The basal body pool contains IFT subcomplexes or individual proteins rather than entire IFT particles, as different IFT proteins occupy distinct spatial territories within the pool.
evaluation: Claims C107 and C35 are supported by imaging data showing distinct spatial distributions of different IFT proteins (Figure 1A, C31-C34). The inference that the pool contains subcomplexes rather than complete particles (C107) is reasonable based on the spatial segregation, though direct biochemical evidence is not provided.

result: The transitional fibers are required to recruit kinesin-2 but not IFT particle proteins to the basal body pool, and kinesin-2 addition is a late step in train assembly, with binding regulated by phosphorylation.
evaluation: Claims C108-C112 integrate prior knowledge (C108-C111, properly cited) with current findings (C112, supported by gap analysis showing short KAP-GFP gap duration). The integration of prior structural/biochemical knowledge with the current functional data strengthens the mechanistic understanding of train assembly.

result: The IFT81/74 module is the dominant tubulin binding site of IFT, with both proteins being core structural components of the IFT-B1 complex, and mutations in both domains impair cilia assembly.
evaluation: Claims C120-C123 accurately describe prior work on tubulin binding by IFT proteins, properly citing multiple studies (Bhogaraju et al., 2013; Kubo et al., 2016; Taschner et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017b; Lucker et al., 2005; Taschner et al., 2014). This provides important context for interpreting the tubulin loading results.

result: Axonemal cargoes are released at the ciliary tip during train disassembly, and cargo binding/unloading may be linked to train assembly and disassembly processes.
evaluation: Claim C125 is well-supported by multiple citations describing cargo release at the tip. Claim C126 is explicitly stated as speculation and represents a hypothesis linking cargo dynamics to train assembly/disassembly, which is reasonable but lacks direct experimental support.
